sections.title: Explanation
sections.body:
> **In one line:** Monitoring is the continuous, automated observation of a system's behavior through metrics, logs, and traces, organized around service-level objectives so that operators can detect, diagnose, and recover from incidents before users are meaningfully affected.
Monitoring is the umbrella discipline that turns raw observability data — billions of metrics, trillions of log lines, sampled traces — into actionable situational awareness. A service that emits metrics but has no dashboard is not monitored; a service with a dashboard but no alerting is monitored passively, which is to say not monitored at all during off-hours. Monitoring is the practice of selecting which signals matter, organizing them into dashboards that humans can scan in seconds, and binding alerts to the signals whose breach means a user is being harmed. Google's SRE book frames it crisply: monitoring exists to answer two questions — "what is broken?" and "why?" — and the quality of a monitoring system is measured by how fast and accurately it answers those questions during an incident. Netflix's Atlas, Uber's M3+Grafana stack, and Google's internal Monarch are all multi-billion-dollar investments in answering those two questions at scale.

The foundational concept in modern monitoring is the service-level objective (SLO). An SLO is a numerical target for the reliability of a service, expressed as the fraction of requests that meet a quality bar over a window. For example: "99.9% of `/checkout` requests will return 200 in under 800ms over any 28-day window." SLOs are derived from user experience research: what latency does a user perceive as "fast enough" to not abandon? What error rate translates to a measurable drop in conversion? At Google, the SLO is set just slightly above the user-visible pain threshold — if the SLO is 99.9%, the team targets 99.95% in steady state but treats the 99.9% line as the cliff. This creates a deliberate "error budget" — the 0.1% of requests that may fail without breaching the SLO — which the team can spend on deployments, experiments, and risk-taking. When the budget is exhausted, feature launches freeze until reliability is restored. This transforms monitoring from "are things up?" into "are we honoring our contract with users?", which is the only framing that aligns engineering trade-offs with business priorities.

The two complementary monitoring philosophies are white-box and black-box. White-box monitoring observes internal state — application metrics, log lines, runtime profiling, JVM heap usage. It is high-fidelity and tells you exactly what is happening inside the service, but it requires instrumentation in every component and is blind to failures outside the instrumented boundary. Black-box monitoring observes the system from outside, as a user would — synthetic transactions that hit the public endpoint, measure latency, and check the response. It is lower-fidelity (you see "request failed" but not why) but it catches the failures white-box misses: DNS outages, certificate expirations, network partitions, load balancer misconfigurations. A mature monitoring system uses both: black-box to catch user-visible failures and trigger paging, white-box to diagnose the cause. Google's SRE book emphasizes that black-box monitoring should be the primary alerting source because it measures user-visible behavior, while white-box is for diagnosis — a counterintuitive rule that many teams violate by alerting on white-box signals (CPU > 80%, heap > 70%) that do not always correspond to user-visible impact.

The three pillars of observability — logs, metrics, traces — are the data sources monitoring operates on. Metrics are the alerting substrate: cheap to store, fast to evaluate, perfect for "is the error rate above threshold?" Logs are the forensic substrate: full event detail, perfect for "what happened in this specific failing request?" Traces are the diagnostic substrate: causal path across services, perfect for "which downstream service was slow, and how much time did it consume?" A modern incident workflow uses all three in sequence: the metric alert fires ("error rate p95 above 1% for 5 minutes"), the engineer opens the dashboard and sees the spike, queries traces for slow/error requests in that window, finds the specific failing trace, and pulls the corresponding logs to see the exact error message. Grafana, Datadog, and Honeycomb have all converged on providing all three pillars in a single pane because the workflow's value comes from the linkage between them — clicking a metric spike should jump to the traces in that window, clicking a trace should jump to the logs of that request.

Dashboards are the human-facing surface of monitoring. A good dashboard answers a single question per panel — "what is the current error rate?" — and arranges panels in priority order from "is the service up?" at top to "what is the breakdown by route?" below. The anti-pattern is the dashboard with 50 panels of unrelated metrics, which overwhelms the on-call engineer during an incident and hides the relevant signal. Google's SRE book recommends the "golden dashboard" pattern: one dashboard per service showing the Four Golden Signals (Latency, Traffic, Errors, Saturation) at the top, dependency health below, and resource utilization at the bottom — all on one screen, no scrolling required during an incident. Netflix's internal dashboarding tool, Telltale, enforces this by requiring each dashboard to declare its primary user question and rejecting dashboards that try to answer multiple unrelated questions.

The real-world cautionary tale is the 2019 Cloudflare outage. A bad regex deploy caused CPU spikes on every edge server worldwide, taking down a meaningful fraction of the internet for 27 minutes. Cloudflare's monitoring correctly detected the spike within seconds, but the alert fired on every server simultaneously, generating 4,000+ pages to the on-call team in under a minute. The team could not even acknowledge the pages fast enough, let alone diagnose the cause. The lesson, codified as "alert on symptoms, not causes" and "route by service, not by host," is that monitoring must be designed for human cognition under stress: a single clear page per incident, not a flood. Cloudflare restructured their alerting to deduplicate by symptom and to roll up per-service rather than per-host, which is now industry standard practice.

The trade-off in monitoring design is coverage versus signal-to-noise. Every metric you collect costs storage and adds cognitive load; every alert you add risks fatigue if it fires spuriously. Mature monitoring teams treat their dashboard inventory and alert rules as code, version-controlled and code-reviewed, with periodic audits to delete unused dashboards and silence noisy alerts. The goal is not "monitor everything" but "monitor the right things at the right fidelity" — a discipline that takes years to develop and is the single biggest differentiator between teams that operate reliable systems and teams that do not.

### Mermaid Diagram
```mermaid
flowchart TD
    A[Service emits metrics/logs/traces] --> B[Three Pillars Store]
    B --> C[Metrics: alerting substrate]
    B --> D[Logs: forensic substrate]
    B --> E[Traces: diagnostic substrate]
    F[Black-box prober] --> G[External view: user-visible]
    H[White-box instrumentation] --> I[Internal view: diagnostic]
    C --> J[Dashboard: Four Golden Signals]
    D --> J
    E --> J
    G --> K[Alert: symptom-based]
    C --> K
    K --> L[On-call engineer]
    L -->|click spike| E
    L -->|click trace| D
```

### ASCII Diagram
```
+---------+      metrics        +-------------+
| Service |  -----------------> |  Prometheus |
|         |  logs               |  Loki       |
|         |  -----------------> |  Jaeger     |
|         |  traces             +-------------+
+---------+  ----------------->        |
                                     query
                                       |
                                       v
                          +-------------------------+
                          |   Dashboard (Grafana)   |
                          |  +-------------------+  |
                          |  | Latency p50/p95   |  |  <-- Four Golden
                          |  +-------------------+  |      Signals
                          |  | Traffic (req/s)   |  |
                          |  +-------------------+  |
                          |  | Errors (%)        |  |
                          |  +-------------------+  |
                          |  | Saturation (CPU)  |  |
                          |  +-------------------+  |
                          +-------------------------+
                                       |
                            alert if SLO burn
                                       v
                          +-------------------------+
                          |  Alertmanager -> Pager  |
                          +-------------------------+
```

### Walkthrough
1. The service emits metrics, logs, and traces; each is stored in its respective backend (Prometheus, Loki, Jaeger).
2. A black-box prober (e.g., synthetic /health check) independently verifies user-visible availability from outside the trust boundary.
3. Grafana renders a dashboard per service showing the Four Golden Signals at the top, dependencies in the middle, resources at the bottom — one screen, no scrolling.
4. Alert rules evaluate metrics against SLO-derived thresholds; when a symptom is detected, Alertmanager deduplicates and routes a single page per incident.
5. The on-call engineer opens the dashboard, sees the spike, clicks through to traces (which service was slow?) and then to logs (why?), recovering in minutes.

sections.title: Code
sections.body:
```python
# monitoring_dashboard.py - runnable; renders a text dashboard from metrics
import random, time
from dataclasses import dataclass, field

@dataclass
class ServiceMetrics:
    name: str
    rate: float          # requests/sec
    error_rate: float    # fraction 0-1
    p50_ms: float
    p95_ms: float
    p99_ms: float
    cpu: float           # 0-1
    mem: float           # 0-1
    slo: float = 0.999    # 99.9% success
    window_events: int = 0
    window_errors: int = 0

    def availability(self) -> float:
        if self.window_events == 0:
            return 1.0
        return 1 - (self.window_errors / self.window_events)

    def slo_burn_rate(self, window_minutes: int = 60) -> float:
        """1.0 = burning budget exactly as planned for the window."""
        budget = (1 - self.slo) * self.window_events
        if budget == 0:
            return 0
        return self.window_errors / budget

def render_dashboard(services: list[ServiceMetrics]) -> str:
    lines = ["=" * 78, "  SERVICE DASHBOARD - Four Golden Signals", "=" * 78]
    lines.append(f"{'SERVICE':<14}{'RATE':>8}{'ERR%':>7}{'P50':>7}{'P95':>7}{'P99':>7}{'CPU%':>7}{'SLObrn':>8}")
    lines.append("-" * 78)
    for s in services:
        err_pct = s.error_rate * 100
        burn = s.slo_burn_rate()
        flag = " OK" if burn < 1 else " !!"
        lines.append(f"{s.name:<14}{s.rate:>8.0f}{err_pct:>6.2f}{s.p50_ms:>6.0f}m{s.p95_ms:>6.0f}m{s.p99_ms:>6.0f}m{s.cpu*100:>6.0f}{burn:>8.2f}{flag}")
    lines.append("=" * 78)
    return "\n".join(lines)

def simulate(service: ServiceMetrics):
    # accumulate a 60-minute window of events
    for _ in range(60):
        events = int(service.rate * 60)
        errors = int(events * service.error_rate)
        service.window_events += events
        service.window_errors += errors

if __name__ == "__main__":
    services = [
        ServiceMetrics("api-gateway",  5000, 0.001,  20,  80, 200, 0.45, 0.55),
        ServiceMetrics("orders-svc",    800, 0.005,  50, 200, 600, 0.72, 0.68),
        ServiceMetrics("payments-svc",  300, 0.020,  80, 350, 900, 0.91, 0.82),
        ServiceMetrics("inventory-svc", 1200, 0.0005, 15,  50, 150, 0.30, 0.40),
    ]
    for s in services:
        simulate(s)
    print(render_dashboard(services))
    # highlight payments-svc which is burning SLO budget 20x faster than allowed
```
